## Pulleys, block and tackle, treadwheel crane `block_and_tackle`
- Deps: helped by lever_mechanics_statics, gears_gear_trains
- Core idea: A rope over a single fixed pulley only changes the direction of the pull. Run the rope back and forth between a fixed block and a block that moves with the load, and the pull needed is the load divided by the number of rope parts holding the moving block; the rope must be hauled that many times further. Each sheave adds bearing friction and bends the rope, so the actual advantage falls short of the ideal by an amount that depends on the tackle. For heavy lifts the rope end goes to a windlass or to a treadwheel, a drum on the axle of a wheel 4 to 5 m across in which men walk: two men then lift several tonnes. A crane needs a ratchet or brake so that the load cannot run back and spin the wheel.
- Pitfalls: Counting pulleys instead of the rope parts on the moving block | Ignoring friction and the stretch and strength of the rope | No brake or pawl on a treadwheel: a slipping load throws the walkers round inside it | Assuming the pyramids were built with pulleys; Old Kingdom Egypt had none
- History: mesopotamia: c. 870 BC – single pulley shown on an Assyrian relief from Nimrud; greece: c. 515 BC – cranes with winch and pulley replace ramps in temple building; 3rd c. BC compound pulley attributed to Archimedes (Plutarch's story of the ship is legend-like); rome: c. 25 BC – Vitruvius describes three- and five-sheave tackles; c. 100 AD treadwheel crane on the tomb of the Haterii; china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – pulleys discussed in the Mohist canon; windlasses and pulleys at Han brine wells; europe: c. 1225 – treadwheel crane reappears in France; 1244 harbour crane at Utrecht; 1420–1421 Brunelleschi's ox-driven reversible hoist for the dome of Florence
- Read: Vitruvius, De architectura X.2 | J. J. Coulton, Lifting in Early Greek Architecture, Journal of Hellenic Studies 94 (1974) | Frank D. Prager & Gustina Scaglia, Brunelleschi: Studies of His Technology and Inventions (1970)

## Wheelbarrow `wheelbarrow`
- Core idea: A box or frame with one wheel and two handles lets one person move what otherwise needs two with a hand barrow, and passes along planks and narrow paths. It is a lever with the wheel as fulcrum. With a small wheel at the front (European type) the pusher still carries a third to a half of the weight; with a large wheel in the middle and the load packed on both sides of it (Chinese type) the wheel carries nearly everything, the pusher only balances and steers, and loads of 150 kg and more are usual.
- Pitfalls: Load placed near the handles instead of over the wheel | A narrow wheel on soft ground; lay planks | Assuming it is too obvious to be missing; Europe built for centuries without it
- History: greece: 408–406 BC – building accounts from Eleusis list a 'one-wheeler' (Lewis reads it as a wheelbarrow; isolated and disputed); china: c. 1st c. BC–2nd c. AD – wheelbarrows on Han tomb reliefs in Sichuan (dated example 118 AD); the attribution to Zhuge Liang (c. 231) is legend for an improved army barrow; sails added later; europe: c. 1170–1250 – first mentions and pictures in England and France; the supposed wheelbarrow in a Chartres window is a hand barrow
- Read: M. J. T. Lewis, The Origins of the Wheelbarrow, Technology and Culture 35 (1994) | Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)

## Archimedes' screw (water screw) `archimedes_screw`
- Deps: helped by crank_connecting_rod, windmill
- Core idea: A spiral partition inside a tube, laid sloping with its lower end in the water and turned about its axis, carries water upward in the pockets between the turns. Vitruvius's recipe: a wooden core as many feet long as it is fingers thick (16 to 1), eight spiral walls built up from pitch-soaked willow strips, the spiral advancing its own diameter per turn, cased in tarred planks bound with iron hoops, and set on the slope of a 3-4-5 triangle (about 37 degrees). It moves a large volume up a small height, 1 to 3 m per screw, and does not mind mud; for more height use several in steps. It is turned by treading, by a crank, or by a windmill.
- Pitfalls: Setting it too steep: above about 45 degrees the pockets spill and nothing arrives | Expecting a high lift from one screw | Leaky joints between spiral and casing | Taking Archimedes' authorship as proven; it is an ancient attribution
- History: mesopotamia: c. 700 BC – Sennacherib's inscription on casting bronze devices to raise water at Nineveh, read by Dalley as water screws; disputed; egypt: c. 250 BC – in use in the Nile delta; ancient writers credit Archimedes, who visited Alexandria; rome: 1st c. BC–2nd c. AD – draining mines in Spain, where wooden screws survive; described by Vitruvius; europe: 15th c. – revived by Italian engineers; 1634 wind-driven screw mills drain Dutch polders; china: 1612 – introduced by the Jesuit Sabatino de Ursis and Xu Guangqi (Taixi shuifa)
- Read: Vitruvius, De architectura X.6 | Stephanie Dalley & John Peter Oleson, Sennacherib, Archimedes, and the Water Screw, Technology and Culture 44 (2003) | John Peter Oleson, Greek and Roman Mechanical Water-Lifting Devices: The History of a Technology (1984)

## Gears and gear trains `gears_gear_trains`
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: Two toothed wheels in mesh turn in opposite directions at speeds inversely proportional to their numbers of teeth, and the turning force changes the other way: a 10-tooth pinion driving a 60-tooth wheel gives one sixth the speed and six times the torque. In a compound train, successive pairs sharing intermediate shafts multiply their ratios, allowing clocks to count turns and cranes to multiply torque. A simple idler changes direction or spacing but cancels out of the speed ratio. Mill gearing uses a face wheel with wooden pegs and a lantern pinion of rods between two discs to turn the drive through a right angle; a worm (screw) driving a wheel gives a large reduction in one step and may resist back-driving if its lead angle is small enough for friction to hold. Teeth must be evenly spaced, by dividing the circle carefully. For quiet, lasting gears the tooth flanks must be curved (cycloid or involute) to maintain a constant speed ratio even as the flanks slide past each other.
- Pitfalls: Uneven spacing, laid out by eye; the wheels jam or knock | Triangular or square teeth for power: they rub, wear fast and run unevenly | Tooth numbers with a common factor in wooden mill gears, so the same teeth always meet and wear unevenly; millers added a 'hunting cog' | Forgetting that gaining force loses speed in the same ratio
- History: greece: 3rd c. BC – gearing in the Alexandrian school (Ctesibius, Archimedes); c. 2nd–1st c. BC Antikythera mechanism with at least 30 bronze gears; rome: c. 25 BC – right-angle gearing of the water mill (Vitruvius); china: c. 3rd c. BC–Han – bronze and iron gear and ratchet wheels; 3rd c. AD Ma Jun's south-pointing chariot; 1088–1094 Su Song's astronomical clock tower; islamic: c. 1000 – al-Biruni's geared calendar; 11th c. al-Muradi, segmental and epicyclic gears; 1206 al-Jazari; europe: c. 1300 – geared mechanical clocks; 1364 de Dondi's astrarium; 1694 La Hire on cycloidal teeth; 1754–1765 Euler on the involute; gear-cutting engines from the 1670s
- Read: T. Freeth et al., Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism, Nature 444 (2006) | Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965) | Donald R. Hill, A History of Engineering in Classical and Medieval Times (1984)

## Cam and camshaft `cam_camshaft`
- Deps: helped by water_wheel
- Core idea: A cam is a projection or shaped disc on a rotating shaft that pushes a lever or rod aside once per turn and then lets it go or guides it back. Pegs on a water wheel shaft lift a hammer, a stamp or a bellows board and drop it; several cams set at different angles round one shaft work several hammers in turn and spread the load evenly. A smoothly shaped cam gives any timed motion wanted: the tunes of a musical automaton, the valves of an engine. It is the simplest way to turn rotation into repeated strokes, needing no crank.
- Pitfalls: All cams in line, so every hammer lifts at once and the wheel stalls | A sharp-edged cam and follower that dig into each other; round and grease them | Expecting a cam to push a heavy load both ways; it lifts, and weight or a spring returns
- History: greece: 3rd c. BC–1st c. AD – cams in Alexandrian automata (Philo, Hero); china: c. 20 AD – cam-lifted water-powered trip hammers (Huan Tan); rome: 1st–2nd c. AD – cam-driven ore stamps inferred from worn anvil stones at Spanish and Welsh gold mines; islamic: 1206 – al-Jazari's camshafts in automata and water-raising machines; europe: 11th–12th c. – cams in fulling and hammer mills; 15th c. stamp mills and pegged-barrel musical automata
- Read: Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965) | al-Jazari, The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206; tr. Donald R. Hill, 1974)

## Screw, nut and bolt `screw_nut_bolt`
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A screw is a slope wrapped round a cylinder. A single-start thread advances by one thread spacing (the pitch) per full turn, so a long handle and a fine pitch turn a small push into an enormous squeeze or a very fine adjustment: the principle of presses, vices, clamps, jacks and measuring instruments. To lay out a first screw, wrap a right-angled triangle of paper or thin metal round the rod and cut along its sloping edge; the nut is cast or cut to match. A screw and nut hold parts together and can be undone again, which nails and rivets cannot. Until threads are cut on a lathe to agreed sizes, every nut fits only its own bolt and they must be marked in pairs.
- Pitfalls: Assuming screws were always around as fasteners; metal screws and nuts are rare before the 15th c. and costly until the 19th | A pitch so steep that the screw runs back under load | Mixing up nuts and bolts made by hand, or by different workshops | Assuming China had it; the screw was the one basic machine element absent there until the 17th c.
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – invention ascribed to Archytas (weak late tradition); 3rd c. BC water screw; 1st c. AD Hero describes screw presses and a tool for cutting internal threads; rome: 1st c. AD – screw presses for oil and wine, 'invented within the last hundred years' (Pliny, Natural History XVIII); small bronze screws in instruments; europe: 15th c. – metal screws in armour, clocks and presses; a screw-cutting lathe drawn in the Mittelalterliches Hausbuch (c. 1480); 1760 Wyatt brothers' screw-making machine; 1841 Whitworth proposes a standard thread; americas: 1864 – William Sellers's standard thread for the United States; china: 17th c. – screw introduced by the Jesuits
- Read: Hero of Alexandria, Mechanica III (in A. G. Drachmann, The Mechanical Technology of Greek and Roman Antiquity, 1963) | Witold Rybczynski, One Good Turn: A Natural History of the Screwdriver and the Screw (2000)

## Belt, rope and chain drives `belt_drive`
- Deps: helped by spinning_wheel, textile_fibres
- Core idea: An endless band round two wheels carries rotation from one shaft to another some distance away. The speeds are in inverse proportion to the diameters, so a large wheel driving a small pulley gives high speed (a spinning wheel's spindle, a lathe); crossing the band reverses the direction. A flat leather belt stays on a pulley whose rim is slightly higher in the middle (crowned), because a belt climbs towards the larger diameter. A belt slips under overload, which protects the machine. A chain on toothed wheels cannot slip and keeps exact timing. In a factory one water wheel or engine turns a long overhead shaft from which each machine takes its drive by a belt, with a loose pulley beside the fast one for stopping.
- Pitfalls: Flat or hollow pulley rims: the belt runs off. The rim must be crowned | A belt too slack or too tight; and damp changes the length of leather and rope | Unguarded belts and shafts, a chief cause of factory injuries
- History: china: c. 15 BC – belt-driven quilling wheel for silk mentioned by Yang Xiong; 976 and 1090 chain drive in the astronomical clocks of Zhang Sixun and Su Song; islamic: 1206 – al-Jazari's chain-of-pots machines; belt-driven spinning wheel shown in Baghdad in 1237; europe: c. 1280 – spinning wheel band drive; c. 1430 belt-driven grindstone; 1790s line shafting in cotton mills; 1880 Renold's bush roller chain; americas: 1828 – Paul Moody at Lowell replaces gear shafting by leather belts, afterwards the American standard
- Read: Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965) | Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)

## Ball and roller bearings `ball_bearings`
- Deps: helped by precision_measurement, crucible_steel, machine_tools, bessemer_steel
- Core idea: A shaft that rolls on balls or rollers has a tenth or less of the friction of one sliding in a greased hole, and starts easily from rest. Early turntables could use wooden rollers or bronze balls. In a fast shaft bearing, the rolling elements must be round and closely matched so they share the load. Hardened, ground races resist indentation, and a cage can keep the elements apart. For most machines before the bicycle the right answer is a plain bearing: a polished iron journal in a bronze or tin-alloy shell, kept flooded with oil.
- Pitfalls: Soft or unequal balls: one large ball carries the whole load, crushes and jams | Assuming a cage carries the shaft load; the rolling elements and races carry it. Some slow, full-complement bearings dispense with a cage | Dirt and no lubricant; rolling bearings still need a little oil and a seal | Fitting them to wooden machinery when a greased bronze bush would do
- History: rome: c. 40 AD – a turntable on bronze balls and wooden rollers on Caligula's ships at Lake Nemi; europe: c. 1500 – Leonardo sketches a caged ball bearing (Codex Madrid I); c. 1750 John Harrison's caged roller bearing in his third sea clock; 1794 Philip Vaughan's patent for ball-bearing carriage axles; 1869 Jules Suriray's patent, used on racing bicycles; 1883 Friedrich Fischer's ball-grinding machine at Schweinfurt; 1907 Wingquist's self-aligning bearing (SKF); americas: 1839 – Isaac Babbitt's tin-based plain bearing metal; 1898 Timken tapered roller bearing
- Read: Duncan Dowson, History of Tribology (1979)

## Bellows and the double-acting piston blower `bellows_piston_blower`
- Deps: helped by water_wheel, cam_camshaft, crank_connecting_rod
- Core idea: A fire's heat depends on its air supply; a strong steady blast is what lifts a furnace from red to white heat and makes iron run. A simple bellows blows only on the closing stroke, so smiths use two in turn. The Chinese box bellows blows on both strokes: a long wooden box with a piston packed with feathers or soft paper, an inlet flap valve at each end, and an air channel along the side with a swinging flap leading to one nozzle. Push or pull, one side fills while the other delivers. Worked by a water wheel through cams or a crank, bellows give the continuous blast a blast furnace needs; later, cast-iron blowing cylinders replace leather.
- Pitfalls: No inlet valve, so the bellows sucks flame and hot gas back from the fire | A puffing, interrupted blast, which will not hold smelting heat | Leather that dries and cracks, or a nozzle that reaches into the fire without a clay tuyere
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – pot bellows with skin covers; earlier smelters used blowpipes; egypt: c. 1450 BC – foot-worked pot bellows in the tomb of Rekhmire; china: 31 AD – Du Shi's water-powered blowers for iron furnaces; double-acting piston bellows certain by the Song (Needham argues for the 4th c. BC from texts; disputed); africa: 1st millennium BC onward – bowl and bag bellows in iron smelting; also tall natural-draught furnaces without bellows; americas: pre-Columbian – no bellows; Andean smelters use blowpipes and wind-blown furnaces (huayras); europe: c. 13th–14th c. – water-powered bellows make the blast furnace possible; c. 1550 wooden box bellows at Nuremberg; 1760s Smeaton's cast-iron blowing cylinders at Carron
- Read: Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965) | Donald B. Wagner, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 5 Part 11: Ferrous Metallurgy (2008)

## Water-powered trip hammer and stamp mill `trip_hammer_water_powered`
- Deps: needs water_wheel, cam_camshaft; helped by bloomery_iron
- Core idea: Cams on the shaft of a water wheel press down the tail or lift the head of a pivoted hammer beam and let it fall, 60 to 150 blows a minute, tirelessly. The same motion with vertical stamps crushes ore, pounds rags to paper pulp, hulls rice, fulls woollen cloth and beats flax. In the forge a heavy helve hammer (100 to 300 kg) works blooms of iron into bars, a lighter fast one draws them out. The hammer head, anvil block and the pivot take the punishment; the anvil needs a deep foundation of timber or stone.
- Pitfalls: A weak pivot or a shallow anvil foundation: the hammer shakes the building apart | Cams that strike the beam instead of sliding under it | No way to stop the hammer quickly while the wheel runs (prop or sluice)
- History: china: 1st c. BC – foot-worked tilt hammer; c. 20 AD water-powered (Huan Tan, Xin lun); rows of hammers on one shaft by the 3rd c.; rome: 1st–2nd c. AD – water-driven pestles in Italy (Pliny, reading debated) and ore stamps at mines in Spain and at Dolaucothi, Wales; islamic: by the 10th–11th c. – water-driven stamps for paper pulp, rice and ore (extent debated); europe: late 11th c. – fulling mills in Normandy; 12th–13th c. forge hammers, spread by Cistercian houses; c. 1280 paper stamp mills at Fabriano
- Read: Adam Lucas, Wind, Water, Work: Ancient and Medieval Milling Technology (2006) | Georgius Agricola, De re metallica (1556; tr. H. C. Hoover & L. H. Hoover, 1912) | Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)

## Lost-wax casting `lost_wax_casting`
- Deps: needs copper_bronze; helped by fired_brick_ceramics
- Core idea: Model the object in beeswax; for a hollow casting lay the wax a few millimetres thick over a clay core and fix the core with metal pins. Add wax rods for the pouring channel and for vents that let air escape. Coat the wax with fine clay slip, then thicker layers of clay mixed with sand and chaff, and dry it fully. Heat the mould upside down so the wax runs out, bake it hard, and pour the metal while the mould is still hot. Break the mould, cut off the channels and finish the surface. Every casting needs a new wax model, but any shape can be made, undercuts included. The metal takes exactly the place of the wax.
- Pitfalls: A mould that is still damp or holds wax: steam blows the metal out, often into the founder's face | No vents, so trapped air leaves holes | Core not pinned, so it shifts and the wall comes out thin or open | Metal too cool or mould cold: the pour freezes before it fills (Cellini's near-disaster with the Perseus)
- History: india: c. 4500–4000 BC – copper amulet from Mehrgarh, Baluchistan, the oldest confirmed lost-wax casting; mesopotamia: 4th millennium BC – Nahal Mishmar hoard (southern Levant) and early Mesopotamian figurines; egypt: 3rd millennium BC onward – statuettes; large hollow bronzes later; greece: 6th–5th c. BC – large hollow statues cast in sections; china: c. 6th–5th c. BC – added to the older piece-mould tradition (Zeng Hou Yi vessel, 433 BC; extent debated); americas: c. 1st millennium BC onward – gold and tumbaga casting in Colombia, later Central America and Mexico; africa: 9th–10th c. AD – Igbo-Ukwu bronzes, Nigeria; Ife and Benin from the 12th–13th c.; europe: c. 1122 – Theophilus describes bell and censer casting; 1545–1554 Cellini's Perseus in Florence
- Read: Benvenuto Cellini, Treatises on Goldsmithing and Sculpture (1568; tr. C. R. Ashbee, 1898) | L. B. Hunt, The Long History of Lost Wax Casting, Gold Bulletin 13 (1980) | M. Thoury et al., High spatial dynamics-photoluminescence imaging reveals the metallurgy of the earliest lost-wax cast object, Nature Communications 7 (2016)

## Sand and loam moulding for large castings `sand_loam_casting`
- Deps: helped by copper_bronze, blast_furnace_cast_iron, lost_wax_casting
- Core idea: For repeated castings, ram damp sand with a little clay round a wooden pattern in a two-part box, lift the halves apart, take the pattern out, cut a pouring channel and risers, and close the box again; a baked sand core makes a hollow. The pattern is reused. For large round things (bells, cannon, pots, engine cylinders) build the mould in loam, a paste of clay, sand and horse dung or chopped straw, struck to shape with a profile board turning on a spindle: first the core, then a false layer the thickness of the metal, then the outer cope; take the false layer out, dry everything by fire and bury the mould in a pit to resist the pressure. Metal shrinks on cooling (cast iron about 1 %, bronze 1.5 %), so patterns are made oversize and risers feed the shrinking casting.
- Pitfalls: Wet moulds or a damp pit: steam explosions with molten metal | No allowance for shrinkage, and no risers, so the casting is undersize and has cavities | A core that floats up in the heavy liquid metal unless anchored | Sharp inside corners and sudden changes of thickness, where castings crack as they cool
- History: mesopotamia: 4th millennium BC – open stone and clay moulds; china: c. 1600–1050 BC – Shang ritual bronzes cast in sectional ceramic piece-moulds; 5th–3rd c. BC cast-iron tools made in stacked and in iron permanent moulds; india: c. 400 AD and later – large iron and bronze founding; c. 1000 Chola bronzes (lost wax); europe: c. 1122 – Theophilus on bell founding in loam; 1540 Biringuccio on cannon and bells; 1707 Abraham Darby's patent for casting iron pots in sand; 1720s loam-moulded iron engine cylinders at Coalbrookdale
- Read: Theophilus, On Divers Arts (c. 1122; tr. J. G. Hawthorne & C. S. Smith, 1963) | Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540; tr. C. S. Smith & M. T. Gnudi, 1942)

## Wire drawing `wire_drawing`
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron; helped by crucible_steel, water_wheel
- Core idea: Point the end of a soft metal rod, push it through a tapered hole in a hard steel plate (the drawplate) and pull the rest through with tongs, a windlass or a water-driven crank; it comes out thinner, longer and exactly round. Repeat through a row of holes each about a tenth smaller in diameter. Drawing hardens the metal, so after a few passes the wire must be annealed (heated to red and cooled slowly) or it snaps. Grease, wax or soap in the hole is essential. Wire makes pins, needles, nails, mail armour, card teeth for wool, springs, strings and later cables and telegraph lines.
- Pitfalls: Too big a reduction per pass, or no annealing: the wire breaks | Dry drawing; the wire welds to the plate and scores | Iron with slag threads in it splits in the plate; wire needs the cleanest iron | Brass and iron wire need different annealing; brass must not be worked hot
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – gold wire made by hammering and by twisting cut strips (Ur); egypt: 2nd millennium BC – strip-twisted and hammered wire in jewellery; true drawing in antiquity is not proven; europe: 8th–10th c. – iron drawplates in Viking-age finds; c. 1122 Theophilus describes the drawplate; c. 1350–1415 water-powered wire mills at Nuremberg; 1540 Biringuccio illustrates them; islamic: early medieval – drawn gold and silver wire for textiles; dates uncertain
- Read: Theophilus, On Divers Arts (c. 1122; tr. J. G. Hawthorne & C. S. Smith, 1963) | W. A. Oddy, The Production of Gold Wire in Antiquity, Gold Bulletin 10 (1977) | Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540; tr. C. S. Smith & M. T. Gnudi, 1942)

## Rolling and slitting mill `rolling_mill`
- Deps: needs gears_gear_trains, screw_nut_bolt; helped by water_wheel, puddling_wrought_iron, blast_furnace_cast_iron
- Core idea: Two hard, smooth, parallel rolls turning in opposite directions draw hot metal between them and squeeze it thinner and longer, far faster and more evenly than a hammer. The gap is set by screws at each end and reduced a little at each pass; the rolls must be thick and their housings massive, or they bend and the sheet comes out thick in the middle. Grooves cut in the rolls turn out round or square bars and later rails. In the slitting mill a second pair of shafts carrying interleaved discs cuts the rolled strip into rods for nails. Rolled plate is what boilers, tinplate and ships' hulls are made of.
- Pitfalls: Thin or badly supported rolls that spring apart | Rolling iron too cold: it cracks at the edges and breaks the mill | Unequal gap at the two ends, so the strip curves | Fingers and clothing drawn into the nip
- History: europe: c. 1480–1500 – Leonardo draws rolls for lead and tin strip; 1550s roller mills for coin strip (Augsburg, Paris); c. 1590 slitting mill brought from the Liège region to Dartford, England; c. 1697–1728 John Hanbury rolls iron sheet for tinplate at Pontypool; 1783 Henry Cort's patent for grooved rolls; 1820 Birkinshaw's rolled wrought-iron rails; americas: 1920s – continuous wide hot-strip mill
- Read: H. R. Schubert, History of the British Iron and Steel Industry from c. 450 B.C. to A.D. 1775 (1957) | R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976)

## Precision cylinder boring `boring_machine`
- Deps: helped by water_wheel, sand_loam_casting, gears_gear_trains, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A cast cylinder is never round or straight inside, and a piston cannot seal in it. To correct it, a cutter head must travel along a path fixed by the machine, not by the rough hole. A stiff iron bar passes right through the cylinder and turns in bearings at both ends; the cutter head slides along the bar, fed by a rack or screw, while the cylinder is clamped still without being squeezed out of shape. Earlier mills, with the cutter on the end of an overhung bar resting on a shoe inside the bore, followed every error of the casting. Wilkinson's large engine bores let Watt seal full-size pistons without excessive friction or steam leakage. Inspect the diameter at several depths and orientations: a bore can have the right diameter at its mouth and still be tapered or oval further in.
- Pitfalls: A cutter guided by the hole it is cutting: it copies the error | A bar supported at one end only, which sags and chatters | Clamping a thin cylinder tightly; it springs back oval when released | Thinking a Newcomen engine needs this; it managed with hand-scoured bores and a water seal, Watt's commercial engines benefited from much closer fits
- History: europe: 1540 – Biringuccio shows water-powered reaming of cored cannon; 1713–1740s Jean Maritz bores cannon from the solid, vertically then horizontally; c. 1770 Smeaton's cylinder boring mill at Carron; 1774 John Wilkinson's cannon-boring patent; 1775 his cylinder boring mill at Bersham, used for Boulton and Watt's engines; china: none known before the 19th c.; bronze and iron guns were cast with a cored bore
- Read: L. T. C. Rolt, Tools for the Job: A Short History of Machine Tools (1965) | H. W. Dickinson & Rhys Jenkins, James Watt and the Steam Engine (1927)

## Screw-cutting lathe with slide rest `lathe_screw_cutting`
- Deps: needs screw_nut_bolt, gears_gear_trains; helped by crank_connecting_rod, belt_drive, crucible_steel, blast_furnace_cast_iron
- Core idea: On a lathe the work turns and the tool is held against it. On the old pole lathe the turner holds the tool by hand; accuracy depends on his skill. The industrial lathe has three things. An all-iron bed with straight guideways. A slide rest: a carriage that clamps the tool and moves it along and across by screws, so the cut is governed by the machine. And a long, accurate lead screw geared to the spindle through exchangeable wheels, which moves the carriage a fixed distance for every turn of the work. With that the lathe cuts true cylinders and screw threads of any pitch, copies the accuracy of its own lead screw, and can make a better lead screw for the next lathe. A first good screw is made by correcting a hand-cut one, using a long nut that averages its errors.
- Pitfalls: A wooden bed or frame; it flexes and the work comes out tapered | Trying to cut threads freehand with a chasing tool for precision work | Play (backlash) in the screws: always approach the cut from the same side | Saying Maudslay invented the slide rest or the screw-cutting lathe; he combined known elements into the standard machine
- History: egypt: c. 300 BC – earliest picture of a lathe, tomb of Petosiris; turned objects are older in the eastern Mediterranean; china: lathe-turned work from the Warring States and Han periods; no screw-cutting; europe: 13th c. – pole lathe pictured; c. 1480 Mittelalterliches Hausbuch shows a screw-cutting lathe with a cross slide; 1569–1578 Jacques Besson; c. 1751–1760 Vaucanson's iron slide-rest lathe; 1770s Ramsden's screw-cutting lathes for instrument screws; 1795 Senot; c. 1797–1800 Henry Maudslay's all-metal lathe with slide rest, lead screw and change gears; americas: 1798 – David Wilkinson's slide-rest lathe patent, Rhode Island
- Read: Robert S. Woodbury, History of the Lathe to 1850 (1961) | L. T. C. Rolt, Tools for the Job: A Short History of Machine Tools (1965)

## Precision measurement (flat surfaces, gauges, micrometer) `precision_measurement`
- Deps: helped by lathe_screw_cutting, screw_nut_bolt, standard_weights_measures, decimal_fractions
- Core idea: Accuracy starts from a flat surface, and flatness can be made from nothing. Take three iron plates; coat one thinly with pigment, rub it on another, scrape down the marked high spots, and work through all three pairs in turn. Two plates can fit while one is hollow and one rounded, but three that all fit each other must be flat. From the plate come straight edges and squares. Sizes are then fixed by hardened gauges: a plug and a ring, or a 'go' and a 'not go' gauge, which any workman can use without reading a scale. A micrometer measures with a fine screw: at 40 threads to the inch (or 0.5 mm pitch) and a head divided into 25 (or 50) parts, one division is a thousandth of an inch (a hundredth of a millimetre). The vernier, a second scale with ten divisions in the space of nine, reads tenths of a division. Iron grows by about a hundredth of a millimetre per metre for each degree, so fine work is compared at one agreed temperature.
- Pitfalls: Lapping only two plates together; they end as matching curves | Trusting a ruler and the eye for fits; the clearance for a sliding fit depends on shaft size, load, lubrication and temperature | Measuring warm work with a cold gauge, or screwing a micrometer down hard | Each workshop keeping its own inch or foot: parts from two towns will not fit
- History: china: 9 AD – bronze sliding caliper with scale (reign of Wang Mang); egypt: 3rd millennium BC – cubit rods, plumb line and square; the Great Pyramid's base is level to about 2 cm; europe: 1631 – Pierre Vernier's scale; c. 1638 William Gascoigne's screw micrometer for telescopes; 1772 Watt's bench micrometer; c. 1805 Maudslay's 'Lord Chancellor' reading to a ten-thousandth of an inch; 1840 Whitworth publishes the three-plate method (in use in Maudslay's shop earlier) and promotes gauges; 1848 Palmer's hand micrometer; 1896 Johansson's gauge blocks (Sweden); americas: 1851 – Brown and Sharpe vernier caliper; 1867 their pocket micrometer
- Read: Joseph Whitworth, Miscellaneous Papers on Mechanical Subjects (1858) | Chris Evans, Precision Engineering: An Evolutionary View (1989) | Simon Winchester, Exactly: How Precision Engineers Created the Modern World (2018)

## Machine tools (planer, shaper, milling machine) `machine_tools`
- Deps: needs lathe_screw_cutting, precision_measurement; helped by high_pressure_steam, crucible_steel, belt_drive
- Core idea: Machine tools are the machines that make machine parts, and their rule is that the machine, not the hand, guides the cutter. The lathe makes round surfaces. The planer makes flat ones: the work is bolted to a table that slides to and fro on straight ways under a fixed single-point tool, which is stepped sideways after each stroke (in the smaller shaper the tool moves instead). The milling machine feeds the work past a rotating cutter with many teeth and produces flats, grooves and shaped profiles, identical every time; it is the key to making gun and sewing-machine parts alike. Drilling, boring and later grinding machines complete the set. Each generation of machine tools is built on the last and can be more accurate than it, because straightness and flatness come from scraping to a reference plate.
- Pitfalls: Light frames: a machine tool must be many times stiffer than the cut seems to need, or it chatters | Expecting hand filing and chiselling to give flat surfaces for steam-tight joints at any reasonable cost | Carbon steel cutters run too fast lose their hardness; before 1900 cutting speeds are a few metres a minute | Crediting single inventors: planer and miller appeared in several workshops at once
- History: europe: 1751 – Nicolas Focq's planing machine in France; c. 1802–1807 Bramah, and Brunel and Maudslay's block-making machines at Portsmouth; c. 1817 Richard Roberts's planer (also Fox, Murray, Clement); 1836 Nasmyth's shaper; 1839–1842 steam hammer; 1830s–1850s Whitworth's standardised tools; americas: c. 1816–1820 – milling machines in the federal armouries and their contractors (Simeon North, John Hall; credit to Eli Whitney is doubtful); 1840s–1850s turret lathe; 1862 Brown and Sharpe universal milling machine; 1900 Taylor and White's high-speed steel
- Read: Joseph Wickham Roe, English and American Tool Builders (1916) | L. T. C. Rolt, Tools for the Job: A Short History of Machine Tools (1965)

## Interchangeable parts `interchangeable_parts`
- Deps: needs precision_measurement; helped by machine_tools, lathe_screw_cutting, standard_weights_measures, division_of_labour
- Core idea: Make every part of a product so nearly alike that any one fits any assembly without filing. Then a broken lock, wheel or gun is repaired from a box of spares, and assembly needs no skilled fitter. The method: a master model; a set of hardened gauges for every dimension of every part, with a 'go' and a 'not go' limit; jigs and fixtures that hold the piece and guide the tool so that the result does not depend on the workman; special machines for each operation; and inspection of every part against the gauges. Parts must be finished after hardening or allowance made for it, since heat treatment distorts them. It costs more than craft work at first and pays only in large numbers.
- Pitfalls: Crediting Eli Whitney: his 1801 demonstration was staged and his muskets were not interchangeable | Working to a drawing or by eye without limit gauges | Gauges that wear and are never checked against a master set | Expecting it to be cheaper from the start; armouries paid a premium for decades to get field repair
- History: china: c. 210 BC – bronze crossbow trigger parts of the Qin army made closely alike in standardised workshops; true interchangeability is claimed but not shown; europe: 1720s – Christopher Polhem's gauged clock wheels at Stjärnsund, Sweden; 1765 Gribeauval's standardised artillery carriages; 1785 Honoré Blanc shows interchangeable musket locks to Jefferson in Paris; 1803–1805 Portsmouth block mills; americas: 1824–1827 – John Hall's breech-loading rifles at Harpers Ferry, the first fully interchangeable arms; 1840s Springfield Armory; 1850s 'the American system' spreads to clocks, sewing machines and reapers
- Read: David A. Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932 (1984) | Merritt Roe Smith, Harpers Ferry Armory and the New Technology: The Challenge of Change (1977) | Ken Alder, Engineering the Revolution: Arms and Enlightenment in France, 1763–1815 (1997)

## Assembly line and mass production `assembly_line`
- Deps: needs interchangeable_parts, division_of_labour; helped by machine_tools, belt_drive, dynamo_electric_motor
- Core idea: Break the making of a product into short steps, place the machines and workers in the order of the steps, and move the work past them at a fixed pace on a chain or belt, so that nobody walks, fetches or waits. Parts must fit without adjustment, or the line stops at the first bad one. Every station must take the same time, so long jobs are split or doubled. At Ford's Highland Park works the time to assemble a chassis fell from about twelve and a half man-hours to about one and a half between 1913 and 1914. The price is monotony: labour turnover reached 370 % in 1913 until wages were doubled to five dollars a day.
- Pitfalls: A line fed with parts that need fitting | One slow station holds up all the others; the line must be balanced | Ignoring the workers: mass quitting, absenteeism and sabotage | A product made in numbers too small to pay for the special machines
- History: china: 3rd c. BC – Qin workshops make weapons and the terracotta army from standard modules; later the Jingdezhen porcelain works pass each piece through dozens of hands; europe: 15th–16th c. – the Venice Arsenal fits out galleys in sequence along a canal; 1803–1805 Portsmouth block mills: 45 machines, ten men doing the work of 110; americas: 1860s – overhead 'disassembly' lines in Cincinnati and Chicago meat packing; 1901 Olds's staged assembly; 1913 moving line at Ford's Highland Park plant
- Read: David A. Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932 (1984) | Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922)

## Water-powered sawmill `sawmill`
- Deps: needs water_wheel; helped by crank_connecting_rod, cam_camshaft, windmill, gears_gear_trains
- Core idea: A crank on the water wheel's shaft, through a connecting rod, drives a rectangular frame holding one or several straight saw blades up and down between guide posts. The log lies on a carriage that is pushed forward a few millimetres at every stroke by a ratchet wheel worked from the saw frame. The teeth cut on the down stroke only. One mill saws as many planks as twenty or more pairs of pit sawyers. Thin circular blades came later and need good steel plate and high speed.
- Pitfalls: Advancing the carriage too far per cycle; the teeth cannot clear the cut and the blade can buckle. Some frame saws advance the log on the return stroke | A slack blade; it must be stretched tight in the frame | Teeth without set (bent alternately left and right), so the blade jams in the cut | Sawyers' guilds: early mills were wrecked or banned in several countries
- History: rome: 3rd c. AD – water-driven stone saws with crank and connecting rod (Hierapolis relief); c. 370 Ausonius hears marble saws on a tributary of the Moselle; europe: c. 1204 – sawmill recorded at Évreux, Normandy; c. 1230 Villard de Honnecourt sketches a saw driven by cams with a spring-pole return; 1593 Cornelis Corneliszoon patents a wind-driven sawmill in Holland; 1777 Samuel Miller's circular saw patent; 1808 Newberry's band saw patent; islamic: 10th c. – water-driven saws reported from al-Andalus; evidence thin; americas: 1620s–1630s – water sawmills in the English and Dutch colonies
- Read: T. Ritti, K. Grewe & P. Kessener, A relief of a water-powered stone saw mill on a sarcophagus at Hierapolis and its implications, Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007) | Terry S. Reynolds, Stronger than a Hundred Men: A History of the Vertical Water Wheel (1983)

## Spinning wheel `spinning_wheel`
- Deps: needs textile_fibres; helped by belt_drive
- Core idea: A large wheel turned by hand drives a small horizontal spindle through a cord, so the spindle makes twenty or more turns for one of the wheel. The spinner holds prepared fibre at an angle to the spindle tip and draws it out while the twist runs into it, then moves the hand so the yarn winds on, and repeats. It yields two to three times as much yarn per hour as the hand spindle. The flyer, a U-shaped arm turning round a bobbin that runs slightly slower or faster, twists and winds on at the same time without stopping; a treadle with a crank frees both hands. Spinning stayed the bottleneck of cloth making: one weaver used the yarn of several spinners.
- Pitfalls: Fibre not carded or combed first; lumps make weak, uneven yarn | Thinking the wheel replaced the hand spindle at once; wheel yarn was at first softer and was banned for warp in some towns | Flyer and bobbin driven at the same speed, so nothing winds on | Crediting the treadle to 'Johann Jürgen of Brunswick, 1530'; that is a later legend
- History: china: wheels for reeling and quilling silk from Han times or earlier; spindle wheel for spinning certain by the 11th c., pictured c. 1270; 1313 multi-spindle treadle wheels in Wang Zhen's Nong shu; india: origin there often asserted, but the first unambiguous reference is of 1350 (Isami); Habib argues it arrived from Iran; islamic: by c. 1030 in use; 1237 earliest clear picture, Baghdad (al-Hariri's Maqamat). Place of invention disputed between the Islamic world, India and China; europe: c. 1280 – first evidence (Speyer guild rules of 1298 allow wheel-spun yarn for weft only); c. 1480 flyer and bobbin (Hausbuch; Leonardo); treadle in the 16th c.
- Read: Dieter Kuhn, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 5 Part 9: Textile Technology: Spinning and Reeling (1988) | Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962) | Patricia Baines, Spinning Wheels, Spinners and Spinning (1977)

## Spinning machines (jenny, water frame, mule) `spinning_machines`
- Deps: needs spinning_wheel, gears_gear_trains; helped by water_wheel, belt_drive, rotative_steam_engine, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: Three ways to spin many threads at once. The jenny copies the hand: a row of upright spindles, and a sliding clamp bar that grips all the loose slivers and draws them out while the spindles twist; then the bar returns and the yarn winds on. It gives soft yarn, by hand power. The water frame draws the fibre out between pairs of rollers, each pair turning faster than the one before, the upper rollers weighted and the pairs set a little further apart than the fibre length, then twists it with a flyer; it runs continuously, needs power and gives strong warp yarn. The mule puts rollers on the frame and spindles on a carriage that runs out and in, and spins the finest yarn. Each needs an even supply of prepared fibre; hand carding serves a small jenny, while a large mill needs mechanised carding to keep up.
- Pitfalls: Rollers set closer than the fibre length break the fibres; too far apart and the sliver falls to pieces | Building the spinning machine and forgetting carding and roving | Trying it first on wool or flax; cotton is the easy fibre, the others took decades more | Attributing roller drafting to Arkwright alone; Lewis Paul and John Wyatt patented it in 1738
- History: china: 1313 – Wang Zhen describes a water-driven frame with 32 spindles for twisting ramie; it did no drafting and was not adapted to cotton; europe: 13th c. – water-driven silk-throwing mills at Lucca and Bologna; 1721 Lombe's silk mill at Derby; 1738 Paul and Wyatt's rollers; c. 1764 James Hargreaves's jenny (patent 1770); 1769 Richard Arkwright's water frame, Cromford mill 1771; 1779 Samuel Crompton's mule; 1825–1830 Roberts's self-acting mule; india: to c. 1800 – hand-spun Bengal cotton sets the standard of fineness the machines had to reach; americas: 1790 – Samuel Slater's mill at Pawtucket on Arkwright's system; 1828 ring spinning (John Thorp)
- Read: Richard L. Hills, Power in the Industrial Revolution (1970) | Robert C. Allen, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (2009)

## Horizontal treadle loom `treadle_loom`
- Deps: needs textile_fibres; helped by spinning_wheel
- Core idea: Cloth is made by passing a weft thread across between two sets of stretched warp threads and then exchanging the sets. On the treadle loom the warp runs horizontally from a warp beam to a cloth beam, so cloth of any length can be wound on. Each warp thread passes through an eye in a heddle; the heddles hang on two or more shafts joined to foot treadles, so pressing a treadle raises one set of threads and lowers the other. The hands are free to throw the shuttle through the opening and to pull the reed, a hanging comb that keeps the threads evenly spaced and beats each weft against the cloth. It weaves several times faster than the upright looms it replaced; more shafts give twills and patterns.
- Pitfalls: Uneven warp tension, which gives baggy stripes and broken threads | No reed, so the cloth narrows and the edges pull in | Unsized, fuzzy warp yarn that chafes through in the heddles
- History: egypt: c. 4400 BC – horizontal ground loom pictured on a dish from Badari (no treadles); china: c. 2nd c. BC – pattern loom models in a tomb at Laoguanshan, Chengdu; 1st–2nd c. AD treadle looms on Han stone reliefs; india: pit treadle loom for cotton; date of origin uncertain, well established by the medieval period; islamic: early medieval – treadle and draw looms for silk across Iran, Syria and Spain; africa: c. 11th c. – narrow-strip treadle weaving in West Africa (Tellem textiles, Mali); americas: pre-Columbian – backstrap and staked looms without treadles; the treadle loom arrives with the Spanish; europe: 10th–11th c. – horizontal treadle loom replaces the warp-weighted loom in towns; broadloom for two weavers in the 13th c.
- Read: Eric Broudy, The Book of Looms: A History of the Handloom from Ancient Times to the Present (1979) | Feng Zhao et al., The earliest evidence of pattern looms: Han Dynasty tomb models from Chengdu, China, Antiquity 91 (2017)

## Flying shuttle and power loom `power_loom`
- Deps: needs treadle_loom, cam_camshaft; helped by spinning_machines, rotative_steam_engine, belt_drive
- Core idea: Flying shuttle: the shuttle runs on small wheels along a ledge on the beater and is knocked from side to side by leather drivers in a box at each end, jerked by a cord in the weaver's hand. One weaver can now make wide cloth alone and about twice as fast. The power loom takes all the motions from one driven shaft: cams lift the shafts, a spring or cam throws the shuttle, a crank swings the beater, a ratchet winds the cloth forward. The real difficulty is what a weaver does without thinking: the loom must stop itself when the weft breaks or runs out and when the shuttle fails to arrive, or it smashes hundreds of warp threads; and the warp must be sized with starch paste beforehand so that it survives the rubbing.
- Pitfalls: No stop motions for a broken weft or a trapped shuttle | Unsized warp; the first power looms had to be stopped constantly to dress it | Speeding up weaving without more yarn: the flying shuttle made the yarn shortage worse | Underrating the resistance: Kay's house was attacked, and weavers broke looms in 1812 and 1826
- History: europe: c. 1580–1604 – multi-ribbon 'engine' looms at Danzig and Leiden, restricted by several towns; 1733 John Kay's flying shuttle; 1745 Vaucanson's automatic loom; 1785–1787 Edmund Cartwright's power loom patents; 1803 Radcliffe and Johnson's warp dressing machine; 1803–1813 Horrocks's loom; 1822 Roberts's iron power loom; americas: 1814 – Francis Cabot Lowell's power loom at Waltham; 1894 Northrop's automatic weft-replenishing loom; east_asia: 1924 – Sakichi Toyoda's automatic loom with shuttle change, Japan
- Read: Richard L. Hills, Power in the Industrial Revolution (1970) | Robert C. Allen, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (2009)

## Cotton gin `cotton_gin`
- Deps: needs textile_fibres; helped by gears_gear_trains, crank_connecting_rod
- Core idea: Cotton fibre has to be separated from its seeds before spinning. The roller gin passes the cotton between two small hard rollers, turning against each other and set closer than a seed is thick: the fibre is pinched through, the seeds are squeezed back. It is gentle and works well for long-fibred cotton with smooth seeds. Short-fibred upland cotton clings to its fuzzy seeds; for it a drum set with wire hooks, or with toothed saw discs, drags the fibre through slots in a grid too narrow for the seeds, and a second drum of brushes turning faster sweeps the fibre off the teeth. One small hand-cranked machine cleans as much as many people picking by hand.
- Pitfalls: Saying Whitney invented the cotton gin; roller gins had been in use in India for over a thousand years | Leaving out the brush drum, so the teeth clog at once | Slots too wide (seeds pass and are cut up) or too narrow (fibre is torn) | Not foreseeing the consequence: cheap ginning made slave-grown cotton hugely profitable and slavery in the United States grew from about 700,000 people in 1790 to 4 million in 1860
- History: india: early centuries AD – single roller on a flat stone (Ajanta paintings, c. 5th c.); two-roller gin with worm gearing and crank (charkhi) by c. the 12th–14th c.; china: 1313 – cranked two-roller gin shown by Wang Zhen; islamic: medieval – roller gins spread with cotton growing to Iran, Egypt and Spain; americas: 1793 – Eli Whitney's wire-tooth gin (patent 1794); 1796 Hodgen Holmes's saw gin
- Read: Angela Lakwete, Inventing the Cotton Gin: Machine and Myth in Antebellum America (2003)

## Stocking frame (knitting machine) `knitting_frame`
- Deps: needs wire_drawing; helped by textile_fibres, precision_measurement
- Core idea: Knitting makes cloth from one thread by pulling loops through loops, which gives a stretchy fabric for stockings. The frame has a row of fixed hooked needles, one for each stitch, each hook ending in a springy tip (the beard) that can be pressed into a groove in the shank. The thread is laid across the needles; thin plates between them push it into a loop on every needle; a bar presses all the beards shut, so the old row of loops slides over the closed hooks and off, leaving the new loops hanging through them. One pass makes a whole row, ten or more times faster than hand knitting. A frame has over two thousand parts and needs evenly made needles of springy wire.
- Pitfalls: Trying to copy the motion of two hand needles; the frame works on a different principle | Uneven or soft needles, which drop stitches | Repeating the tale that Queen Elizabeth refused Lee a patent to protect hand knitters; it first appears long afterwards and is not documented
- History: islamic: c. 11th–13th c. – hand-knitted cotton socks from Egypt, the oldest true knitting; europe: 13th–14th c. – hand knitting in Spain and Italy; 1589 (traditional date) William Lee's stocking frame, Nottinghamshire; he took it to Rouen c. 1610; 1758 Jedediah Strutt's rib attachment; 1775 warp knitting; 1811–1812 Luddite frame breaking; 1816 Marc Brunel's circular frame; 1847–1849 Matthew Townsend develops and patents latch needles
- Read: William Felkin, A History of the Machine-Wrought Hosiery and Lace Manufactures (1867) | Richard L. Hills, William Lee and His Knitting Machine, Journal of the Textile Institute 80 (1989)

## Sewing machine `sewing_machine`
- Deps: helped by wire_drawing, cam_camshaft, machine_tools, interchangeable_parts, crank_connecting_rod
- Core idea: In a lockstitch machine the eye is near the point of the needle, so the needle can form a stitch without passing its whole length through the cloth. As it starts back up, the thread bulges into a small loop under the cloth; a shuttle carrying the bobbin passes through the loop, or a rotary hook sweeps the loop around the bobbin case. Pulled tight, the two threads lock in the middle of the cloth (lockstitch). A toothed plate under the cloth moves it on by one stitch length while the needle is up, a sprung foot holds the cloth down, and discs tension the upper thread and a separate spring tensions the bobbin thread. A chain stitch instead draws each loop through the preceding one. Thimonnier used a hooked needle and the operator fed the cloth by hand.
- Pitfalls: Imitating the hand stitch with pincers and a double-pointed needle; decades were lost on this | Giving a lockstitch needle its eye at the blunt end; the hook must catch a loop close to the point | Irregular feed gives uneven stitch lengths; unbalanced thread tensions cause loops or puckering | Timing of hook and needle out by a fraction: skipped stitches
- History: europe: 1790 – Thomas Saint's patent for a chain-stitch leather machine (probably never built); 1814–1839 Josef Madersperger's machines in Vienna; 1830 Barthélemy Thimonnier's chain-stitch machine, 80 in use until tailors wrecked the workshop in 1831; americas: c. 1833 – Walter Hunt's lockstitch machine, not patented; 1846 Elias Howe's patent; 1850–1854 Isaac Singer and Allen Wilson (rotary hook, four-motion feed); 1856 patent pool ends the 'sewing machine war'
- Read: Grace Rogers Cooper, The Sewing Machine: Its Invention and Development (1976) | David A. Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932 (1984)
